lead: Bending loss is the extra attenuation caused when a fiber is curved. On a bend the outer part of the guided field would have to travel faster than light can in the cladding, so that part breaks away and radiates. Two forms exist: macrobending, where the whole fiber follows a visible curve, and microbending, where tiny random wiggles of the axis couple light out along the length. Every installed cable bends at trays, cabinets and wall corners, and the bend rules tell the installer how tight is safe.

blocks.text: Picture the mode field as a wheel spoke turning round the centre of the bend. To keep its phase front straight, the field further out must move faster. At some radial distance, called the radiation caustic, the required speed exceeds c/n₂, the speed of light in the cladding. The field beyond that point cannot keep up and radiates away. A tighter bend moves the caustic closer to the core, where the field is stronger, so the loss climbs very quickly.

Measured loss per turn follows an exponential law well, written α<sub>r</sub> = c₁e<sup>−c₂R</sup>, where R is the bend radius and c₁ (dB per turn) and c₂ (per mm) are fitted from measurements on one fiber at one wavelength. The fit holds over the radii where it was measured; it is not a universal curve.
A rough scale for the radius where loss becomes large is the critical radius. For a multimode fiber:

Rc ≈ 3n₁²λ / [4π(n₁² − n₂²)3/2]
Rc is the critical radius, in the unit of λ; n₁ and n₂ are the core and cladding indices; λ is the free-space wavelength.
For a single-mode fiber the field reaches much further into the cladding, and the estimate becomes

Rcs ≈ [20λ/(n₁ − n₂)3/2] (2.748 − 0.996λ/λc)−3
Rcs is the single-mode critical radius; λc is the cutoff wavelength of the fiber; λ, Rcs and λc share one length unit.

Both formulas say the same thing: a large index difference holds the field tightly and allows sharp bends, and a longer wavelength, which spreads the field, needs gentler ones. Multimode fiber with Δ ≈ 1 % has R<sub>c</sub> of only tens of micrometres; standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm has R<sub>cs</sub> of a few centimetres.

Microbending comes from many small random bends of the axis, with periods of a millimetre or less and amplitudes of micrometres. Uneven coating, cabling pressure, a rough drum surface and thermal contraction of the coating at low temperature all cause them. Each wiggle is tiny, but together they act like a weak grating that couples the guided mode to cladding and radiation modes, so power leaks out evenly along the length. A soft inner coating and a stiff outer coating, which smooths the outside forces, is the usual cure.

blocks.text: Bending loss rises with wavelength. At 1550 nm the mode field is wider than at 1310 nm, so more of it sits beyond the caustic, and the same bend costs more. Installers therefore test bends at 1550 nm or 1625 nm, the worst case. Bend-insensitive fiber adds a low-index trench in the cladding that pulls the mode back toward the core; it is used in drop cables, patch cords and crowded racks.

sections.h3: Using bend loss in a link budget

blocks.text: Macrobend loss is quoted per turn at one radius and one wavelength, so multiply by the number of turns before adding it to the budget. Microbend loss is already spread along the cable and appears inside the cable’s dB/km figure. A mandrel test wraps a set number of turns on a rod of known size and measures the added loss; note that mandrels are specified by diameter, so a 30 mm mandrel gives a 15 mm bend radius.

items: Find the tightest bend radius R on the route.
Read the loss per turn at the working wavelength from the data sheet or a measured curve.
Count the turns N at that radius and add N × α<sub>r</sub> dB to the budget.
If the margin is small, open up R, re-route, or use bend-insensitive fiber.

blocks.text: At 0.2 dB/km, 1 dB of bend loss costs as much as 5 km of fiber, which is why bend rules matter as much as the fiber’s own attenuation.

examples.question: A 1550 nm fiber has a measured bend loss α<sub>r</sub> = 8e<sup>−0.6R</sup> dB per turn, R in mm, valid from 4 to 15 mm. (a) Find the loss of one turn at R = 5 mm and at R = 10 mm. (b) A tray forces four turns at R = 5 mm; find the added loss. (c) The same fiber passes a mandrel test on a 30 mm mandrel; what is the loss per turn?
steps: At R = 10 mm: 0.6 × 10 = 6, e<sup>−6</sup> = 0.002479, α<sub>r</sub> = 8 × 0.002479 = 0.0198 dB per turn. Doubling R cut the loss twentyfold.
(b) Four turns at 5 mm: 4 × 0.398 = 1.59 dB, as much as 8 km of fiber at 0.2 dB/km.
(c) A 30 mm mandrel means R = 15 mm: e<sup>−9</sup> = 1.234 × 10<sup>−4</sup>, α<sub>r</sub> = 8 × 1.234 × 10<sup>−4</sup> = 0.00099 dB per turn, too small to matter.
examples.answer: 0.40 dB per turn at 5 mm and 0.020 dB at 10 mm; four turns at 5 mm add 1.6 dB; on the 30 mm mandrel the loss is about 0.001 dB per turn.

examples.question: Find the critical bend radius (a) of a multimode fiber with n₁ = 1.48 and n₂ = 1.46 at 850 nm, and (b) of a single-mode fiber with n₁ = 1.465, n₂ = 1.460 and cutoff λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.26 µm, at 1550 nm and at 1310 nm.
examples.answer: The multimode fiber can bend to about 31 µm before loss is large; the single-mode fiber needs about 25 mm at 1550 nm and 15 mm at 1310 nm, which is why single-mode bend rules are tested at the longer wavelength.

traps: Saying bend loss is worse at shorter wavelength. It rises with wavelength, so 1550 nm suffers more than 1310 nm at the same radius.
Using the loss per turn as the total. Multiply by the number of turns before adding it to the budget.
Reading a mandrel size as a radius. Mandrels are quoted by diameter; a 30 mm mandrel bends the fiber to R = 15 mm.
Mixing up the two kinds: macrobending is one visible curve, quoted per turn; microbending is many tiny wiggles, quoted in dB/km.
Using the single-mode R<sub>cs</sub> formula without the cutoff wavelength, or putting λ and λ<sub>c</sub> in different units.

quiz.a: Macrobending: loss from a visible curve of radius R. Microbending: loss from many small random bends of the axis, caused by coating, cabling or temperature.

quiz.q: Why does a guided mode lose power on the outside of a bend?
quiz.a: The field further from the centre of the bend must travel faster to keep its phase front. Beyond the radiation caustic it would need more than c/n₂, so that part radiates away.

quiz.q: With α<sub>r</sub> = 8e<sup>−0.6R</sup> dB per turn (R in mm), find the loss of two turns at R = 6 mm.
quiz.a: e<sup>−3.6</sup> = 0.02732, so α<sub>r</sub> = 0.219 dB per turn; two turns give 0.44 dB.

quiz.q: Using the same curve, find the loss of five turns at R = 10 mm.
quiz.a: α<sub>r</sub> = 8e<sup>−6</sup> = 0.0198 dB per turn; five turns give 0.099 dB, about 0.1 dB.

quiz.q: For the single-mode fiber of the second worked example, what happens to R<sub>cs</sub> at 1550 nm if the index difference doubles to n₁ − n₂ = 0.010 (same cutoff)?
quiz.a: (0.010)<sup>3/2</sup> = 1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, so 20 × 1.55 µm ÷ 10<sup>−3</sup> = 31.0 mm; times 0.283 gives 8.8 mm. A larger index step lets the fiber bend about 2.8 times tighter.

quiz.q: Why does a 1550 nm link suffer more bend loss than a 1310 nm link at the same radius?
quiz.a: The mode field is wider at the longer wavelength, so more of it lies beyond the radiation caustic. The critical radius grows with λ: 25 mm against 15 mm for the fiber in the worked example.

quiz.q: How does a low-index trench in the cladding reduce bend loss?
quiz.a: The trench raises the effective index contrast around the core and pulls the mode inward, so less field reaches the caustic on a bend.

beyond: Bend-insensitive single-mode fibers are standardised as ITU-T G.657; the A2 and B3 grades allow radii of 7.5 mm and 5 mm for drop cables and in-home wiring. Data sheets quote macrobend loss at 1550 nm and 1625 nm, the worst cases. Fiber-optic sensors use controlled bending on purpose: a microbend sensor squeezes the fiber between corrugated plates and reads pressure from the extra loss. Search for “G.657 bend-insensitive fiber” and “microbend sensor”.
